data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is indefensible on Popper's own terms and smuggles induction back in by implicitly asserting that past performance is a reliable guide to future reliability, which contradicts the definition of corroboration as a mere historical report.","counterconditions":[{"case":"refuted if a coherent account can be provided where preferring a better-corroborated theory is justified solely as a method to maximize the severity of future tests without any assumption that the theory will actually succeed","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"refuted if Popper explicitly distinguished 'corroboration' as a report of past performance versus 'probability' as a prediction of future frequency in a way that validates action without induction","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"refuted if a definitive textual analysis shows Popper endorsed acting on corroborated theories without any implicit assumption that their past success is relevant to their future performance","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"By advising scientists to prefer the better-corroborated theory for action, Popper implicitly relies on the inductive principle that nature is uniform or that successful methods remain successful, reducing his methodology to a description of psychological habit rather than a logical framework.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
